record.paper_title: Open Problems on Information and Feedback Controlled Systems
record.context_brief: Implications for nano and biological systems
record.original_question: What concrete limitations do information-theoretic and thermodynamic bounds for feedback-controlled systems impose on the operation and achievable performance of nanotechnology devices and biological systems in which one subsystem uses bidirectional interaction with another subsystem to improve that subsystem's performance?

evidence.quote: Thus, the bounds of the performance of the feedback controlled systems will imply limitations to the operation of nanotechnology devices and biological systems. Finding these implications is still a very relevant open question.

artifact.category_tag: feedback control and thermodynamics of information
artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a composite stochastic system consisting of two interacting subsystems X and Y evolving in continuous or discrete time. Subsystem Y acts as a controller that measures the state of X, producing a measurement record with mutual information I(X;Y) per unit time, and then applies a control signal back to X based on this record (bidirectional, feedback interaction). Assume X obeys stochastic thermodynamics: its evolution is described by a Markov dynamics satisfying local detailed balance, with well-defined entropy production, extracted work W, and free-energy change ΔF. For such feedback-controlled systems the generalized second law takes the form
   ⟨W⟩ ≤ −ΔF + k_B T · I,
where I is an appropriate information-theoretic quantity (e.g., the mutual information acquired by the controller, or the transfer entropy rate from X to Y), k_B is Boltzmann's constant, and T is the temperature of the bath.

Problem. Derive concrete, quantitative limitations that the above class of information-thermodynamic inequalities (together with related bounds such as those constraining measurement and erasure costs, transfer-entropy-based second laws, and thermodynamic uncertainty relations) impose on the operation and achievable performance of:
 (i) nanotechnology devices that exploit feedback (e.g., Maxwell-demon-type information engines, single-electron devices, molecular machines), and
 (ii) biological systems in which one subsystem uses bidirectional interaction with another to improve the second subsystem's performance (e.g., sensory adaptation networks, kinetic proofreading, biochemical signaling, molecular motors driven by feedback).

Specifically, identify and prove explicit upper bounds on natural performance measures — such as extracted work, power output, energetic efficiency, sensing precision, adaptation accuracy, or copying fidelity — in terms of the information-theoretic quantities I (mutual information, transfer entropy, or directed information rate) characterizing the bidirectional coupling, and exhibit physically realizable models that saturate these bounds.
artifact.status_search_result: The question, as posed, is a broad programmatic open problem about translating information-thermodynamic feedback bounds into concrete limits on nano-devices and biological systems. Substantial progress has been made on individual instances since 2012 (e.g., Sagawa–Ueda generalized second laws, Barato–Seifert thermodynamic uncertainty relations, information-thermodynamic bounds on sensing, adaptation, and molecular motors), but no comprehensive resolution exists; the general program remains open.

status_evidence.title: Thermodynamics of information
status_evidence.snippet: Review describing generalized second laws for feedback-controlled systems and their applications to small physical and biological systems, noting many open directions.
status_evidence.claim: The general program of deriving concrete performance limits for nano and biological feedback systems from information-thermodynamic bounds is active and incomplete.

status_evidence.title: Thermodynamic uncertainty relation for biomolecular processes
status_evidence.snippet: Derives bounds linking dissipation and precision relevant to biological feedback/sensing systems.
status_evidence.claim: Partial progress exists on specific bounds (TUR) but a general program remains open.
